# Abstract {.unnumbered}

Studies that impute a missing biomarker report the threshold where the averaged Youden curve peaks, without uncertainty, overstating its accuracy. We propose a band for the pooled curve by bootstrap-then-impute, a set of thresholds no other threshold beats beyond their difference's uncertainty, and a bootstrap correction of the index. In simulation, the band covered the curve in `r rng(nrm$cover_hybrid, nrm$cover_hybrid_mcse)` of replicates with normal imputation, but in `r rng(pmm_hi$cover_hybrid, pmm_hi$cover_hybrid_mcse)` with predictive mean matching at `r lvl(100 * max(miss_levels))`% missing, where imputations were biased. The set held the best threshold in `r rng(s$compset_hybrid, s$compset_hybrid_mcse)` at `r span(s$length_ratio_hybrid)` of a band-based set's length. Without missing data the index exceeded the chosen threshold's accuracy by `r rng(nul$optimism, nul$optimism_mcse, 3)`; the correction left `r rng(nul$corrected_bias_20, nul$corrected_bias_20_mcse, 3)`. In NHANES, the cotinine set, `r pr(10^app$real$set_ranges$comp_hybrid[1], 2)` to `r pr(10^app$real$set_ranges$comp_hybrid[2], 2)` ng/mL, held the published `r lvl(app$placement$reference_ng_ml, 2)` ng/mL cutoff.

*Keywords:* multiple imputation; Youden index; optimal cutoff; simultaneous confidence band; multiple comparisons with the best; bootstrap

# Introduction

A threshold on a biomarker decides who is counted as having a condition: a threshold on serum cotinine, a metabolite of nicotine, separates people who smoke cigarettes from people who do not, and its value has been estimated from national survey data [@benowitz2009; @tompkins2019]. One criterion for the best threshold maximizes the sum of sensitivity and specificity, and that sum minus one is the Youden index [@hassanzad2024]. When the biomarker is missing for some participants, multiple imputation, one of the most popular approaches to missing data [@bartlett2020], fills in the missing values several times and analyses each completed dataset. In the paper that proposed nonparametric multiple imputation for ROC analysis, depression screening scores missing for part of a cohort of pregnant women were multiply imputed, the true and false positive rates were averaged across the completed datasets at each threshold, and one score was reported as "the unanimous optimum threshold", with no statement of its uncertainty [@long2011]. Applied studies impute a marker and then report an optimal cutoff [@abdulrahman2022; @atlantis2016; @wirth2024], and the two whose full text was read do not say how the completed datasets were combined [@abdulrahman2022; @atlantis2016]; many studies do not report the precision of their cutpoints at all [@thiele2023].

The reported index overstates the accuracy of the threshold it picks, because the threshold is chosen where the estimated curve happens to be high. With $F_0$ and $F_1$ the distribution functions of the marker among people without and with the condition, and a person called positive when the marker exceeds $c$, the Youden curve, its best threshold, and its maximum are
$$
\begin{aligned}
J(c) &= F_0(c) - F_1(c), \\
c^* &= \arg\max_c J(c), \\
J^* &= J(c^*).
\end{aligned}
$$
From $L$ completed datasets the analyst averages the empirical curves $\hat J_1, \dots, \hat J_L$ into $\bar J$, takes the threshold $\hat c$ at which $\bar J$ peaks, and reports the peak, $\max_c \bar J(c)$. Because $\max_c \bar J(c) \ge \bar J(c^*)$ in every dataset and $J(\hat c) \le J^*$, the reported index exceeds the true accuracy of the chosen threshold on average whenever the averaged curve is unbiased at $c^*$:
$$
\mathrm{E}\{\max_c \bar J(c)\} - \mathrm{E}\{J(\hat c)\} \;\ge\; \mathrm{E}\{\bar J(c^*)\} - J^* \;=\; 0 .
$$
Without missing data the empirical index has the largest upward bias of the usual estimators [@fluss2005], intervals exist for the index and the threshold [@bantis2019], and confidence regions exist for the sensitivity and specificity at the estimated threshold [@bantis2014]. The empirical threshold converges at the cube-root rate to a non-normal limit [CITE: the cube-root rate and the non-normal limit of an argmax of a step criterion (Kim and Pollard 1990; no readable text in Zotero)]{.cite} [@cattaneo2020], as does a weighted Youden threshold [@wang2025weighted]. Rubin's rules assume approximately normal estimates [@leyrat2019], so they do not apply to the threshold, and the standard bootstrap is inconsistent for it [@cattaneo2020]. When the disease status rather than the marker is missing, the ROC curve [@fluss2009] and intervals for the Youden index [@wang2025interval; @jia2026] have been derived. When the marker is missing, imputation methods give the ROC curve and its area [@long2011; @karakaya2015; @cheng2020]. No method gives a band for the Youden curve, a set of thresholds that the data cannot separate from the best one, or a correction of the reported index from multiply imputed data.

This paper proposes all three and asks whether each works. The band estimates the covariance of the averaged curve by bootstrapping the data and imputing each resample [@bartlett2020], and takes a sup-t critical value [@montielolea2019]. The near-optimal set keeps every threshold that no other threshold beats by more than the uncertainty of their difference, in the manner of multiple comparisons with the best [@hsu1996] [CITE: multiple comparisons with the best (Hsu 1984; no PDF in Zotero)]{.cite}. The correction subtracts a bootstrap estimate of the optimism [CITE: the bootstrap estimate of optimism (Efron 1983; Harrell, Lee, and Mark 1996; no readable text in Zotero)]{.cite}, with each resample imputed as many times as the analysis. A simulation study then asks four questions. Does the band cover the whole curve at the nominal rate, under predictive mean matching as well as under a correctly specified imputation model? Does the set contain the best threshold at least as often as its level promises, and how much narrower is it than the set the band itself gives? Does the correction remove the optimism of the reported index? And, as a note on the order of operations, how far apart are the index from averaging the curves first and the index from maximizing in each completed dataset first? An application to serum cotinine and smoking in the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey [CITE: the NHANES 2013 to 2018 data files (no item in Zotero)]{.cite} then asks whether the data can choose between a published cutoff and the cohort's own.

# Methods

## The estimand

The question a threshold answers is how accurate it is, and the question a study answers is which threshold is most accurate. We therefore take as estimand the whole Youden curve and its peak, not one threshold. With $F_d$ the distribution function of the marker $X$ in group $D = d$, and a person called positive when $X > c$, the curve, its best threshold, and its maximum are
$$
\begin{aligned}
J(c) &= F_0(c) - F_1(c), \\
c^* &= \arg\max_c J(c), \\
J^* &= J(c^*).
\end{aligned}
$$
A study that picks a threshold $\hat c$ from data delivers the accuracy $J(\hat c)$, which falls short of $J^*$ by the regret $J^* - J(\hat c)$. The marker is missing for some participants, at random given the disease status and observed covariates, and the disease status is always observed.

## The pooled curve and its index

The analysis completes the data $L$ times and averages the empirical curves of the completed datasets. With $X_i^{(l)}$ the marker of participant $i$ in completed dataset $l$, observed or imputed, and $n_d$ the size of group $d$,
$$
\begin{aligned}
\hat F_{dl}(c) &= n_d^{-1} \textstyle\sum_{i : D_i = d} 1\{X_i^{(l)} \le c\}, \\
\hat J_l(c) &= \hat F_{0l}(c) - \hat F_{1l}(c), \\
\bar J(c) &= L^{-1} \textstyle\sum_{l=1}^{L} \hat J_l(c).
\end{aligned}
$$
The pooled curve $\bar J$ is a step function. The reported index is its maximum, $\max_c \bar J(c)$, and the chosen threshold $\hat c$ is the midpoint of the interval on which the maximum is reached, or the mean of those midpoints when several intervals tie. This is the procedure of Long, Zhang, and Hsu [@long2011], who averaged the curves of the completed datasets. The alternative, maximizing in each completed dataset first, reports the mean of the per-dataset maxima and the mean $\tilde c = L^{-1} \sum_l \hat c_l$ of the per-dataset cutoffs.

At a fixed threshold the pooled curve is an average of differences of two proportions, so it is a regular estimate, and Rubin's rules apply to it under proper imputation [@leyrat2019]. Its maximum is not regular. The reported index exceeds the accuracy the chosen threshold delivers, in expectation, whenever the pooled curve is unbiased at $c^*$; the argument takes two lines (Supplementary note, S1.1). For the empirical curve the excess is of order $n^{-2/3}$, because the empirical threshold converges at the cube-root rate [CITE: the cube-root rate of an argmax of a step criterion (Kim and Pollard 1990; no readable text in Zotero)]{.cite} [@cattaneo2020] (S1.2). Maximizing first adds to that excess a gap that is never negative and is close to $\kappa \hat B_c / 2$, with $\kappa = -J''(c^*)$ the curvature at the peak and $\hat B_c$ the variance of the per-dataset cutoffs (S1.3).

## A band for the curve

A band that contains the whole curve with probability `r lvl(100 * nominal)`% brackets the accuracy of every threshold at once. We estimate the covariance of the pooled curve on a grid by bootstrapping the data and imputing each resample, whose variance estimates hold when the imputation and analysis models are uncongenial [@bartlett2020], and we impute each resample only $M$ times, which is enough when the variance is split into its parts [@vonhippel2021]. The grid holds $K = `r lvl(proc$grid_n)`$ equally spaced thresholds $c_1 < \dots < c_K$ between the `r lvl(100 * grid_probs[1])`% and `r lvl(100 * grid_probs[2])`% quantiles of all completed values. In each of $R_B = `r lvl(proc$n_boot)`$ resamples, drawn with replacement within each disease group, the resample is imputed $M = `r lvl(proc$m_boot)`$ times, giving curves $\hat J_{b1}, \dots, \hat J_{bM}$ on the grid with mean $\bar J_b$. Then
$$
\begin{aligned}
V &= \widehat{\mathrm{Cov}}_b(\bar J_b), \\
W &= R_B^{-1} \textstyle\sum_b (M - 1)^{-1} \sum_m (\hat J_{bm} - \bar J_b)(\hat J_{bm} - \bar J_b)^\top, \\
\Sigma &= V - W / M + W / L,
\end{aligned}
$$
with negative eigenvalues of $\Sigma$ set to zero. Here $V$ is the covariance of an $M$-imputation estimate and $W$ the covariance of one imputation about its resample's mean, so $\Sigma$ is the covariance of the $L$-imputation estimate the analysis reports (S1.4). With $\mathrm{SE}_k = \Sigma_{kk}^{1/2}$, the band is $\bar J(c_k) \pm q\,\mathrm{SE}_k$ for $k = 1, \dots, K$, with a sup-t critical value $q$ [@montielolea2019]. The bootstrap band takes $q$ as the `r lvl(100 * nominal)`% quantile over resamples of $\max_k \lvert \bar J_b(c_k) - m_k \rvert / V_{kk}^{1/2}$, with $m$ the mean of the $\bar J_b$. The hybrid band takes $q$ as the same quantile of $\max_k \lvert Z_k \rvert / \mathrm{SE}_k$ over `r lvl(proc$n_draw)` draws of $Z \sim N(0, \Sigma)$.

We compared both with two bands built from Rubin's rules [@rubin1987]. The pointwise intervals combine, at each threshold, the binomial within-imputation variance of the two proportions with the between-imputation variance. The Rubin's-rules band uses the whole covariance: the within-imputation covariance of an empirical distribution function, $\{F(a) - F(a)F(b)\}/n$ for $a \le b$, plus $(1 + 1/L)$ times the between-imputation covariance of the curves, with a sup-t critical value from the normal law. Because the within-imputation covariance of the empirical curve is known in closed form, this band also stands for imputing first and bootstrapping each completed dataset.

## A set of near-optimal thresholds

The thresholds a study cannot tell apart from the best one are the useful answer to "which threshold", and a band gives a first such set: the thresholds whose upper limit reaches the band's highest lower limit, $\{k : U_k \ge \max_j L_j\}$. That set uses the band's width twice. The comparison-based set compares thresholds with each other, in the manner of multiple comparisons with the best [@hsu1996] [CITE: multiple comparisons with the best (Hsu 1984; no PDF in Zotero)]{.cite}. With $\mathrm{SE}_{jk} = (\Sigma_{jj} + \Sigma_{kk} - 2 \Sigma_{jk})^{1/2}$ the standard error of the difference between thresholds $j$ and $k$, a threshold stays in the set unless another beats it by more than its critical value:
$$
S_C = \{ k : \bar J(c_j) - \bar J(c_k) \le q_D\,\mathrm{SE}_{jk} \text{ for every } j \ne k \}.
$$
Nearby thresholds share most of their errors, so $\mathrm{SE}_{jk}$ is small where $c_j$ is close to $c_k$, and $S_C$ is narrower than the band-based set. For each grid point $k$, let $q_k$ be the `r lvl(100 * nominal)`% quantile of $\max_{j \ne k} (D_j - D_k)/s_{jk}$, over the centred resample means with $s_{jk}$ from $V$ (bootstrap) or over draws of $N(0, \Sigma)$ with $s_{jk} = \mathrm{SE}_{jk}$ (hybrid). The critical value $q_D = \max_k q_k$ guarantees that the grid's best threshold is in the set whenever the comparisons involving it hold (S1.5); the plug-in value $q_D = q_{\hat k}$, at the estimated best grid point $\hat k$, is smaller.

## A correction of the reported index

The bootstrap estimates how far a maximum overshoots by repeating the whole analysis on resamples and measuring each resample's overshoot against the original data [CITE: the bootstrap estimate of optimism (Efron 1983; Harrell, Lee, and Mark 1996; no readable text in Zotero)]{.cite}. In each of $R_O = `r lvl(proc$n_boot_opt)`$ further resamples, drawn within disease groups and imputed $L$ times as the analysis is, we took the resample's pooled curve $\bar J_b$ and its maximizer $\hat c_b$, and computed
$$
\begin{aligned}
o_b &= \bar J_b(\hat c_b) - \bar J(\hat c_b), \\
\hat J_{\mathrm{corr}} &= \bar J(\hat c) - R_O^{-1} \textstyle\sum_b o_b .
\end{aligned}
$$
The correction starts from the pooled curve at the chosen threshold, which equals the maximum unless tied intervals lie apart.
The same correction from the first $`r lvl(proc$n_boot_opt2)`$ curve resamples, imputed $M$ times each, was computed for comparison. The standard bootstrap does not reproduce the distribution of a cube-root estimator [@cattaneo2020], so whether the correction removes the optimism is a question for the simulation, not a property of the method.

## The order of pooling

For the note on the order of operations, we also recorded the mean of the per-dataset cutoffs $\tilde c$ and of the per-dataset maxima, the variance $\hat B_c = L^{-1} \sum_l (\hat c_l - \tilde c)^2$, and a bagged cutoff, the mean of the cutoffs $\hat c_b$ of the $R_O$ correction resamples, the resampling analogue of maximizing first [@zhang2020].

## Data

The application used the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) cycles 2013 to 2014, 2015 to 2016, and 2017 to 2018 [CITE: the NHANES 2013 to 2018 data files (no item in Zotero)]{.cite}: the serum cotinine laboratory files, the smoking questionnaire, and the demographics files, downloaded from the survey's public data pages. The cohort was every participant aged eighteen or over who answered whether they had smoked one hundred cigarettes in their life; a current smoker had, and now smoked every day or some days, and everyone else who answered was a nonsmoker. The three cycles measured cotinine with the same laboratory method and limit of detection, and values below the limit are stored at the limit divided by the square root of two. The marker was log10 cotinine in ng/mL. The cohort held `r cnt(app$n_adults)` adults, `r cnt(sum(app$by_cycle$smokers))` of them current smokers, and cotinine was missing for `r cnt(sum(app$by_cycle$cotinine_missing))` (`r pr(100 * sum(app$by_cycle$cotinine_missing) / app$n_adults, 1)`%).

Missing cotinine was imputed by predictive mean matching [@vanbuuren2011] with five donors on smoking status, age and its square, sex, the interactions of smoking status with age and sex, race/ethnicity, cycle, education, and the ratio of family income to poverty, with refused, unknown, and unasked education and income as their own category. The analysis of the real missing values was repeated on the complete cases without imputation, as a benchmark, and on the complete cases with `r lvl(100 * app$imposed_rate)`% of cotinine values set missing at random, with probability $\mathrm{expit}(\alpha_0 + 0.5 D - 0.3 a + 0.2 m)$, $a$ the standardized age and $m$ the male indicator, so that the complete-case curve is the truth the analysis should recover. For each race/ethnicity group $v$ the analysis was run within the group. Its stratum-specific cutoff maximizes $\bar F_0(c \mid v) - \bar F_1(c \mid v)$. Its population-optimal cutoff maximizes $w_0(v) \bar F_0(c \mid v) - w_1(v) \bar F_1(c \mid v)$, with $w_d(v)$ the group's share of all participants with $D = d$; one such cutoff per group maximizes the Youden index of the whole population (S1.6). No survey weights were used: the estimand is the curve in the sample's population, as in the simulation.

## Software and reproducibility

{{< include parts/reproducibility.md >}}

The analyses used `r r_version` and the R package `mice` version `r mice_version` [@vanbuuren2011] for both imputation engines. [TO CONFIRM: the repository URL, withheld while review is double-anonymized]{.tc}

# Simulation study

## Design

{{< include parts/ademp-sentence.md >}}

*Aims.* The study asked four questions, in the order of the Introduction. Does the bootstrap band, or the hybrid band, cover the whole curve in `r lvl(100 * nominal)`% of replicates, under predictive mean matching as under a correctly specified imputation model? Does the comparison-based set hold the grid's best threshold at least that often, and how long is it? Does the matched correction remove the optimism of the reported index? And how large is the gap between the two orders of pooling, against $\kappa \hat B_c / 2$?

*Data-generating mechanisms.* The marker was normal in each group, $X \mid D = 0 \sim N(0, 1)$ and $X \mid D = 1 \sim N(\delta, \sigma_1^2)$, with an auxiliary variable $Z = X + e$, $e \sim N(0, 1)$, observed for everyone. The marker was missing with probability $\mathrm{expit}(\alpha_0 + Z + 0.5 D)$, at random given $Z$ and $D$, and above all at high values of the marker, where donors for predictive mean matching are sparse; $\alpha_0$ was solved for each target fraction. @tbl-design lists the factors varied, their levels, and the reason for each. The design had five arms, `r lvl(nrow(design))` cells in all: the three shapes at `r lvl(n_base)` per group, each with a cell without missing values and the three missing fractions crossed with the two main imputation engines; the sharp shape at `r paste(lvl(setdiff(n_sizes, n_base)), collapse = " and ")` per group with the same cells; the sharp shape with ten donors, and with complete cases, at the three missing fractions; and the sharp shape with `r lvl(unb$n1)` cases and `r lvl(unb$n)` controls. Fixed were $L = `r lvl(proc$n_imp)`$ imputations, the empirical estimator, the auxiliary's strength, and the missingness coefficients, as in an applied analysis with one strong auxiliary. In every cell without missing values the completed datasets are identical, so the bands are complete-data bands and the gap between the orders of pooling is exactly zero.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-design
#| tbl-cap: !expr cap_design

design_table(design_rows, widths = c(16, 44, 40))
```

*Estimands.* The Youden curve $J$ on each replicate's grid, the grid's best threshold $c_{k^*}$ with $k^* = \arg\max_k J(c_k)$, the maximum $J^*$, and the accuracy $J(\hat c)$ of the chosen threshold.

*Methods.* In every replicate, the procedure of the Methods with $L = `r lvl(proc$n_imp)`$, $K = `r lvl(proc$grid_n)`$, $R_B = `r lvl(proc$n_boot)`$ resamples with $M = `r lvl(proc$m_boot)`$ imputations each, and $R_O = `r lvl(proc$n_boot_opt)`$ correction resamples: the pointwise intervals, the Rubin's-rules band, the bootstrap band, and the hybrid band; the band-based set and the comparison-based set of each construction, the latter with the largest and with the plug-in critical value; the reported index, the matched correction, and the two-imputation correction; the pooled, averaged, and bagged cutoffs. Predictive mean matching used type 1 matching with five or ten donors, and normal imputation drew the regression parameters and then the missing values; both used $D$, $Z$, and $D \times Z$ as predictors [@vanbuuren2011]. Complete cases ran the same procedure without imputation on the participants with the marker observed.

*Performance measures.* For each band, its simultaneous coverage, the share of replicates in which it contained the true curve at every grid point, and its mean half-width. For each set, the share of replicates in which it held $c_{k^*}$, its mean length (the number of grid points times the grid step), and its length against the band-based set's and against the length of the true range of thresholds within `r lvl(tol_region)` of $J^*$. For each index, its mean minus $J(\hat c)$: the optimism of the reported index, and the bias of each corrected index. For each cutoff, its bias, empirical standard error, and root mean squared error against $c^*$. For the pooling order, the mean gap against the mean of $\kappa \hat B_c / 2$. At $c_{k^*}$, the averaged curve's bias, and the ratio of its Monte Carlo standard deviation to its mean standard error from $\Sigma$ and from Rubin's rules, which tells a biased curve from an underestimated variance. A difference was called nonzero only when it exceeded three Monte Carlo standard errors.

*Replicates.* The study used `r prov(ri$n_rep, 0)` replicates per cell, in seeded blocks so that results do not depend on the computer that ran them; the Monte Carlo standard error of a coverage near `r lvl(nominal)` is then `r prov(sqrt(nominal * (1 - nominal) / ri$n_rep), 3)`. The protocol's production design has `r lvl(ri$n_rep_production)` replicates per cell, a Monte Carlo standard error of `r lvl(sqrt(nominal * (1 - nominal) / ri$n_rep_production), 3)`.

## Results

### The bands

Without missing values the bands are complete-data bands, and the hybrid band covered the whole curve in `r rng(nul$cover_hybrid, nul$cover_hybrid_mcse)` of replicates across shapes, sizes, and balance (@fig-bands). The lowest, `r one(small_null$cover_hybrid, small_null$cover_hybrid_mcse, 2)`, was at `r lvl(min(n_sizes))` per group [TO CONFIRM: whether the band undercovers at 100 per group without missing values; the shortfall from 0.95 is under three Monte Carlo standard errors at 100 replicates]{.tc}. With normal imputation the hybrid band covered in `r rng(nrm$cover_hybrid, nrm$cover_hybrid_mcse)` of replicates and the bootstrap band in `r rng(nrm$cover_boot, nrm$cover_boot_mcse)`. With predictive mean matching the hybrid band covered in `r rng(pmm_lo$cover_hybrid, pmm_lo$cover_hybrid_mcse)` of replicates at `r lvl(100 * miss_levels[2])`% and `r lvl(100 * miss_levels[3])`% missing, and in `r rng(pmm_hi$cover_hybrid, pmm_hi$cover_hybrid_mcse)` at `r lvl(100 * max(miss_levels))`%, lowest for the `r worst$shape` shape. Ten donors in place of five gave `r span(p10$cover_hybrid)` at the three missing fractions. The Rubin's-rules band covered in `r span(nrm$cover_rubin)` of replicates with normal imputation and in `r span(pmm$cover_rubin)` with predictive mean matching, the pointwise intervals read as a band in at most `r prov(max(s$cover_pointwise), 2)`, and the bands of the complete cases in `r span(ccs$cover_hybrid)`.

Where the bands fell short under predictive mean matching, the averaged curve was biased at the best threshold, while its standard error matched its Monte Carlo spread (@tbl-diagnostic). At the grid's best threshold the bias of the averaged curve reached `r one(worst$curve_bias_best, worst$curve_bias_best_mcse)` in the `r worst$shape` shape at `r lvl(100 * worst$miss_rate)`% missing (Table S1). Across every cell with imputed values, the Monte Carlo standard deviation of the averaged curve there was `r span(imp$sd_se_ratio)` times the mean standard error from the bootstrap-then-impute covariance. The same ratio for the Rubin's-rules standard error reached `r prov(max(pmm$sd_se_ratio_rubin), 2)` under predictive mean matching. Under the missingness model, `r lvl(100 * miss_levels[2])`% missing overall meant `r prov(100 * miss_sharp[1, "controls"], 0)`% of controls and `r prov(100 * miss_sharp[1, "cases"], 0)`% of cases for the sharp shape, and `r lvl(100 * max(miss_levels))`% overall meant `r prov(100 * miss_sharp[nrow(miss_sharp), "controls"], 0)`% and `r prov(100 * miss_sharp[nrow(miss_sharp), "cases"], 0)`%.

```{r}
#| label: fig-bands
#| fig-cap: !expr cap_bands
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 10

gap_register("fig-bands", what = "simultaneous coverage of the four bands, every cell", cells = nrow(s), n_rep = ri$n_rep)
PlotBandCoverage(s, s$label)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-diagnostic
#| tbl-cap: !expr cap_diagnostic

gap_register("tbl-diagnostic", what = "bias and SD/SE at the best threshold, sharp shape", cells = nrow(diag_rows), n_rep = ri$n_rep)
kable_w(diag_rows, widths = c(30, 14, 14, 14, 14, 14))
```

### The near-optimal sets

The hybrid comparison-based set held the grid's best threshold in `r rng(s$compset_hybrid, s$compset_hybrid_mcse)` of replicates across all cells, and the bootstrap one in `r rng(s$compset_boot, s$compset_boot_mcse)` (@fig-sets). The hybrid set's length was `r span(s$length_ratio_hybrid)` of the band-based set's, and `r span(s$compset_hybrid_length / s$true_region_length, 1)` times the length of the true range of thresholds whose index is within `r lvl(tol_region)` of $J^*$. Without missing values in the sharp shape, its length fell from `r prov(small_null$compset_hybrid_length, 2)` at `r lvl(min(n_sizes))` per group to `r prov(big_null$compset_hybrid_length, 2)` at `r lvl(max(n_sizes))`. The plug-in critical value, `r span(s$q_plug_hybrid)` across cells against `r span(s$q_comp_hybrid)` for the largest per-point quantile, shortened the hybrid set to `r span(s$length_ratio_plug_hybrid)` of the band-based set's length, and that set held the best threshold in `r rng(s$compplug_hybrid, s$compplug_hybrid_mcse)` of replicates.

```{r}
#| label: fig-sets
#| fig-cap: !expr cap_sets
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 10

gap_register("fig-sets", what = "coverage and length of the near-optimal sets, every cell", cells = nrow(s), n_rep = ri$n_rep)
PlotSets(s, s$label, limit = nominal)
```

### The corrected index

Without missing values the reported index exceeded the true accuracy of the chosen threshold by `r rng(nul$optimism, nul$optimism_mcse, 3)` (@fig-optimism). For the sharp shape the optimism fell with group size, from `r one(small_null$optimism, small_null$optimism_mcse)` at `r lvl(min(n_sizes))` per group to `r one(big_null$optimism, big_null$optimism_mcse)` at `r lvl(max(n_sizes))`, a slope of `r one(slope[["slope"]], slope[["se"]], 2)` on the log scale [TO CONFIRM: the slope lies between minus one half and the minus two thirds of Supplementary note S1.2 within the precision of 100 replicates]{.tc}. The correction with `r lvl(proc$n_imp)` imputations per resample left `r rng(nul$corrected_bias_20, nul$corrected_bias_20_mcse, 3)` in those cells. With normal imputation the optimism was `r rng(nrm$optimism, nrm$optimism_mcse, 3)` and the corrected index's bias `r rng(nrm$corrected_bias_20, nrm$corrected_bias_20_mcse, 3)`. With predictive mean matching the corrected index's bias was `r rng(pmm$corrected_bias_20, pmm$corrected_bias_20_mcse, 3)`, lowest where the averaged curve was most biased. The correction with `r lvl(proc$m_boot)` imputations per resample had a bias of `r rng(s$corrected_bias_2, s$corrected_bias_2_mcse, 3)` across all cells.

```{r}
#| label: fig-optimism
#| fig-cap: !expr cap_optimism
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 10

gap_register("fig-optimism", what = "optimism and corrected-index bias, every cell", cells = nrow(s), n_rep = ri$n_rep)
PlotOptimism(s, s$label)
```

### The order of pooling

Maximizing in each completed dataset first raised the index above the pooled maximum by `r rng(imp$gap, imp$gap_mcse, 4)` in the cells with imputed values (@fig-gap). The gap was `r span(pmm$gap_ratio)` times the mean of $\kappa \hat B_c / 2$ under predictive mean matching and `r span(nrm$gap_ratio)` times under normal imputation. The averaged cutoff's root mean squared error was `r span(imp$rmse_ratio)` of the pooled cutoff's, and the bagged cutoff's `r span(s$rmse_ratio_bag)` (Table S2).

```{r}
#| label: fig-gap
#| fig-cap: !expr cap_gap
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 5

gap_register("fig-gap", what = "pooling-order gap against kappa B_c / 2", cells = sum(s$miss_rate > 0 & s$engine != "cc"), n_rep = ri$n_rep)
PlotGap(s)
```

# Application

## Data and comparison

The application asks the question of the Introduction on real data: which serum cotinine threshold separates people who smoke cigarettes from people who do not, and how sure can a study be of it, when cotinine is missing for some participants. The cohort, its definitions, and the imputation model are in the Methods. Of the `r cnt(app$n_adults)` adults, `r cnt(sum(app$by_cycle$smokers))` were current smokers, and cotinine was missing for `r pr(100 * app$missing_by_status[["1"]], 1)`% of smokers and `r pr(100 * app$missing_by_status[["0"]], 1)`% of nonsmokers. @tbl-placement places the data on the simulation's gradients: the complete-case curve is as high as the separated shape's and as flat at its peak as the flat shape's, the groups are larger than the largest simulated size, and the real missing fraction, spread evenly over the two groups, is below the smallest simulated one, which falls on the cases above all.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-placement
#| tbl-cap: !expr cap_placement

kable_w(placement_rows, widths = c(34, 10, 22, 34))
```

## The data cannot choose between the published cutoff and the cohort's own

With the real missing values imputed, the pooled curve peaked at `r pr(10^app$real$c_hat, 2)` ng/mL, where its index was `r pr(app$real$apparent, 3)` (@fig-application, left). The matched correction lowered the index by `r pr(app$real$optimism_20, 4)`, to `r pr(app$real$corrected_20, 3)`. The comparison-based set of the hybrid construction ran from `r pr(10^app$real$set_ranges$comp_hybrid[1], 2)` to `r pr(10^app$real$set_ranges$comp_hybrid[2], 2)` ng/mL, and that of the bootstrap construction was the same; the band-based set ran from `r pr(10^app$real$set_ranges$band_hybrid[1], 2)` to `r pr(10^app$real$set_ranges$band_hybrid[2], 2)` ng/mL. The adult cutoff of `r lvl(app$placement$reference_ng_ml, 2)` ng/mL published from the 2009 to 2014 cycles [@tompkins2019] lay inside every set. A study that reports the cohort's optimum as the cutoff therefore reports one point of a range that the data cannot narrow further, and the published cutoff, whose complete-case index is lower by `r pr(app$placement$j_star_empirical - app$placement$j_at_reference, 3)`, is as well supported.

With `r pr(100 * app$imposed_share, 1)`% of the complete cases' cotinine values set missing at random, depending on smoking status, age, and sex only, a weaker dependence than the simulation's, the analysis recovered the complete-case curve (@fig-application, right). The bootstrap band, the hybrid band, the Rubin's-rules band, and even the pointwise intervals contained the complete-case curve at every grid point, and every set held the complete-case curve's best grid threshold. The reported index, `r pr(app$imposed$apparent, 3)`, exceeded the complete-case curve at the chosen threshold, `r pr(app$imposed$benchmark$full_at_c_hat, 3)`, by `r pr(app$imposed$apparent - app$imposed$benchmark$full_at_c_hat, 3)`, and the correction removed `r pr(app$imposed$optimism_20, 4)` of it. In this analysis the hybrid comparison critical value rose to `r pr(app$imposed$hybrid$q_comp, 2)`, against `r pr(app$imposed$hybrid$q_comp_plugin, 2)` for the plug-in value, and the hybrid comparison-based set widened to `r pr(10^app$imposed$set_ranges$comp_hybrid[1], 2)` to `r pr(10^app$imposed$set_ranges$comp_hybrid[2], 2)` ng/mL, while the bootstrap and plug-in sets ran from `r pr(10^app$imposed$set_ranges$comp_boot[1], 2)` to `r pr(10^app$imposed$set_ranges$comp_boot[2], 2)` ng/mL.

```{r}
#| label: fig-application
#| fig-cap: !expr cap_application
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4.4

gap_register("fig-application", what = "NHANES pooled curves, bands, and sets", cells = NA, n_rep = NA, run = ari$run, production = "the same analysis")
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4.2, 4.4, 2, 1))
PlotApplication(app$real, reference = log10(app$placement$reference_ng_ml),
                main = "Real missing values imputed")
PlotApplication(app$imposed, benchmark = app$imposed$benchmark$curve,
                reference = log10(app$placement$reference_ng_ml),
                main = "Missing values imposed on the complete cases")
par(op)
```

By race/ethnicity, the stratum-specific cutoffs ranged from `r pr(min(10^app$strata$c_cs), 2)` to `r pr(max(10^app$strata$c_cs), 2)` ng/mL (@tbl-strata), and the published cutoff lay in the comparison-based set of `r pr(sum(app$strata$reference_in_set), 0)` of the `r pr(nrow(app$strata), 0)` groups. The population-optimal cutoff differed from the stratum-specific one in `r pr(sum(abs(app$strata$c_pop - app$strata$c_cs) > 1e-9), 0)` groups, upward where the group held a larger share of the nonsmokers than of the smokers and downward where it held a smaller share, as S1.6 predicts.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-strata
#| tbl-cap: !expr cap_strata

gap_register("tbl-strata", what = "cutoffs by race/ethnicity", cells = NA, n_rep = NA, run = ari$run, production = "the same analysis")
kable_w(strata_rows, widths = c(22, 10, 10, 14, 14, 16, 14))
```

# Discussion

@tbl-novelty sets what this paper adds beside what was known. The four questions of the Introduction have these answers, on `r prov(ri$n_rep, 0)` replicates per cell. Does the band cover the whole curve at the nominal rate, under predictive mean matching as well as under a correctly specified imputation model? Under the correct model, and without missing values, it covered close to the nominal rate; under predictive mean matching it did so at low missing fractions and fell short where the averaged curve itself was biased, at the highest missing fraction. Does the set contain the best threshold at least as often as its level promises, and how much narrower is it than the set the band itself gives? It held the best threshold at least as often as the level promises in every cell, at about half the length of the band-based set, yet still several times longer than the range of thresholds that are truly near-optimal. Does the correction remove the optimism of the reported index? It removed most of it without missing values and under the correct model, and overcorrected where the imputations were biased. How far apart are the index from averaging the curves first and the index from maximizing in each completed dataset first? By a few thousandths of the index, close to $\kappa \hat B_c / 2$, while maximizing first, or bagging, gave a more accurate threshold.

For a study that imputes a missing marker and reports a cutoff, three changes follow. Report the pooled curve with its band and the comparison-based set, so that readers see the range of thresholds the data support, as in the cotinine example, where the published cutoff and the cohort's own both fell in the set. Report the corrected index beside the maximum. And treat the imputation model as part of the inference: the bootstrap-then-impute covariance tracked the curve's variance in every cell, so a band that undercovers points to imputations that are biased near the threshold, which ten donors, the pool recommended against sparse donors [@morris2014], did not fix, and which a correctly specified model avoided [TO CONFIRM: this reading rests on the normal engine being the correct model in the simulation; no misspecified parametric model was tried]{.tc}. Complete cases are not an alternative when missingness depends on the marker's correlates: their bands missed the curve in most replicates.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-novelty
#| tbl-cap: "What was known and what this paper adds. MI is multiple imputation."

novelty_table(data.frame(
  Element = c("The pooled Youden curve from MI data",
              "A simultaneous band for the curve",
              "A set of near-optimal thresholds",
              "The optimism of the reported index",
              "The order of pooling",
              "The bootstrap with MI"),
  `Prior literature` = c(
    "curves averaged across completed datasets, a threshold read off without uncertainty [@long2011]",
    "sup-t bands in general [@montielolea2019]; complete-data intervals for the index and the threshold [@bantis2019]",
    "multiple comparisons with the best [@hsu1996]; confidence regions at the estimated threshold [@bantis2014]",
    "the empirical index biased upward without missing data [@fluss2005]",
    "propensity scores [@mitra2016; @leyrat2019; @granger2019], variable selection [@wood2008], and predictions [@mertens2026] across completed datasets",
    "which combinations are valid [@schomaker2018; @bartlett2020], few imputations per resample [@vonhippel2021]"),
  `This paper` = c(
    "a band, a near-optimal set, and a corrected index for it",
    "a bootstrap-then-impute sup-t band, with the covariance split from two imputations to the analysis's twenty",
    "a set built from comparisons between thresholds on the pooled curve, narrower than the set a band gives",
    "a correction that repeats the imputation as the analysis does, measured under MI",
    "the gap for the Youden index and its quadratic form, measured",
    "applied to a whole curve and to a non-regular maximum"),
  check.names = FALSE), widths = c(20, 40, 40))
```

Several features of the simulation limit what it shows. The marker was binormal, while real markers are skewed or, like cotinine below its limit of detection, carry a point mass; the application has one, the simulation does not. The auxiliary's strength and the missingness coefficients were fixed, so the band's shortfall under predictive mean matching was measured at one level of donor sparsity per missing fraction. The imputation model had one auxiliary and, for the normal engine, was correctly specified; real imputation models carry several covariates and are misspecified to some degree. Missingness was at random given the auxiliary and the disease status, and missingness that depends on the marker's own value is corrected by neither engine. The covariance was always estimated from two imputations per resample and rescaled, and the number of resamples and of imputations per resample was not varied. The set's guarantee is for the grid's best threshold, not for $c^*$ itself, and the grid had one resolution.

Several directions lie outside this paper. A second dataset is needed to test the procedure on a marker with another shape. A continuous covariate turns the stratum-specific cutoffs of the application into a covariate-specific curve [@inacio2017; @xu2014]. When the disease status rather than the marker is missing, the same questions arise under verification bias [@fluss2009; @wang2025interval]. Criteria other than the Youden index, such as a target sensitivity, need their own sets. A bootstrap with a theory for cube-root estimators [@cattaneo2020], carried through imputation, is the candidate for removing the optimism the plain correction leaves. A software release of the procedure, and a short reporting guide for applied studies that impute a marker and report a cutoff, are the steps that make the procedure usable.
